title: No one can purify another (161–166)
hookLine: by oneself evil is done, by oneself one is purified
carry: no one can do it for you

lines: THEY CAN DRIVE YOU TO THE GYM.
cards: Someone can drive you to the gym. They can buy you the shoes, set the alarm, even stand next to you on the treadmill cheering. But they can't do your push-ups for you.
If they do fifty, your arms stay exactly as they were. Everyone knows this about the body. We're less sure about it with the mind.
We'd love for someone to hand us calm, or patience, or a clean conscience, already assembled. Chapter twelve ends with a verse that gently shuts that door.

teach.h: HARM IS EASY; GOOD IS HARD.
teach.b: Verse one sixty-three, in Max Müller's words: "Bad deeds, and deeds hurtful to ourselves, are easy to do; what is beneficial and good, that is very difficult to do." No sugarcoating.
Just before it, verse one sixty-two pictures great wickedness as a creeper that drags down the tree it wraps around.

Then the heart of it, verse one sixty-five: "By oneself the evil is done, by oneself one suffers; by oneself evil is left undone, by oneself one is purified. Purity and impurity belong to oneself, no one can purify another."
The Pali word for purity is suddhi: cleanness, clearness.
The verse is careful and balanced: harm and its undoing, both in your own hands. That's sobering, and some readers find it freeing too: impurity, the verse says, belongs to oneself as well.
Then verse one sixty-six, with a story. The commentary says that when the Buddha announced he would pass away in four months, many monks crowded around him anxiously.

One monk, Attadattha, stayed away and meditated instead. The others complained. Asked why, he said he wanted to reach the goal while the Buddha was still alive, and the Buddha praised him: this is how to honor me.
Don't neglect your own good for another's, the verse says.

teach.h: NO ONE CAN DO IT FOR YOU.
teach.b: That doesn't mean you walk alone. Teachers and friends matter a great deal on this path. But they're the ones driving you to the gym.

how: Buddhists honor teachers, monastics and spiritual friends as essential guides, while holding, as this verse says, that each person must do the work of purifying their own mind.

o: a ritual washing done at a temple
purity, a mind made clean and clear

games.q: match each piece of today's verses.
p: sat in meditation instead of crowding
harm is easy; good is hard

s: verse 165 says a teacher can purify a student
"purity and impurity belong to oneself, no one can purify another."
the Buddha praised the monk who went off to meditate
the commentary says he called it the right way to honor him.
this verse means Buddhists practice entirely alone
teachers and friends matter greatly; they guide, but can't do the work for you.

games.q: the Buddha has said he'll pass away in four months. everyone crowds around him. you're Attadattha. what do you do?
o: go and meditate, to reach the goal while he's alive.
games.why: he went to meditate. the others complained, but the Buddha praised him: that's how to honor the teacher.

practice: Think of one thing you've been waiting for someone else to fix in you: being less anxious once work calms down, or kinder once your family is easier.
Ask what one step you could take yourself, however small; not the whole journey, one step. Then take the step that's already in your hands: this breath, then this one.

wordCard.voice: Suddhi. Purity, cleanness: verse one sixty-five's teaching that by oneself harm is done, by oneself one is purified, and no one can purify another.

orig.note: Pali: purity, cleanness — the word in verse 165 for what no one can give another.

carryVoice: Your line: no one can do it for you. Others can guide; the work itself stays in your hands. Day one hundred ninety.
